delete.title: Delete permission
delete.label: Delete
delete.confirm: Are you sure you want to delete this permission?

restore.title: Restore permission
restore.label: Restore
restore.confirm: Are you sure you want to restore this permission?

help.intro: A permission is a pair - an entity and an operation - that the rest of the application checks by name. The row grants nothing on its own; it becomes access only once it is assigned to an operator from the user screen.
help.step_1_body: The field suggests the entity names the code actually checks; anything typed outside that list is stored as written and read by nobody. Two suggestions are not backend entities - "dashboard" gates the dashboard landing page from this app's middleware, and "account" only keys the public self-service screens.
help.step_2_body: create, read, update, find and delete are what the backend checks, and delete covers restore as well. Holding delete on an entity is also what makes its soft-deleted rows visible in that entity's list at all. Not every entity uses every operation - refund exists for cash-flow entries only.
help.step_3_body: Entity and operation are unique together among rows that are not deleted, and a duplicate is refused with a conflict. If the pair exists but is deleted, whoever holds permission delete gets that row restored instead of a new one; anyone else is told it already exists as deleted.
help.step_4_body: Assignment lives on the user screen, under "Setup permissions", and appears for operators only - members inherit nothing and admins bypass every check, so neither offers it. Nothing done here changes who holds what.
help.step_5_body: Search matches entity and operation from three characters, except for an all-digit term, which is treated as an id and matched exactly. The list can be ordered by id, entity or operation, and nothing else.
help.note: Deleting a permission is a soft delete and takes it away from every operator holding it, because the access check skips deleted rows. The grants themselves are left untouched, so restoring the row hands the permission back to all of them at once. An operator already signed in keeps the old access until their cached permission set is rebuilt.
